question: What does idempotency mean in this scheduler, and why is clientRequestId supplied by the caller instead of generated by the server?
answer_hinglish:
Idempotency ka matlab hai: same operation ko baar baar call karo, result same hi rahega, duplicate side-effect nahi hoga. Yahan caller schedulePost() ko ek clientRequestId deta hai -- agar same id ke saath wahi request dobara aaye (jaise network timeout hone par caller ne retry kiya), scheduler naya post nahi banata, purana wala hi return kar deta hai.

Server-generated id yeh problem solve nahi karta, kyunki caller ko pata hi nahi chalega ki yeh request pehle already gayi thi -- har network call par server ek NAYA id de dega, aur duplicate post ban jayega. Caller ko khud yaad rakhna padta hai ki "main yeh wala request bhej raha hoon", isliye id caller se aata hai, server se nahi.

Real use case: campaign manager ek button click karta hai "Schedule Post", request jaati hai, par response aane se pehle UI timeout ho jaata hai. User phir se click karta hai. Agar dono requests same clientRequestId (jaise button-click-session-id) carry karen, scheduler dusri baar koi naya post nahi banayega -- wahi pehla post return hoga.
why_needed: Network retries, double-clicks aur at-least-once delivery guarantees ki duniya mein, caller side se retry hona normal hai. Agar scheduler khud duplicate detect na kare, user ko same post do baar dikh sakta hai apne LinkedIn par.
real_world_analogy: Restaurant mein order number: waiter order ticket number 47 leke kitchen mein deta hai. Agar waiter confuse ho jaaye aur dobara wahi ticket leke jaaye, kitchen dekhegi ticket 47 already bana raha hai, dusri plate nahi banayegi.
how_it_works: schedulePost() pehle clientRequestId ki shape check karta hai, phir idempotency Map mein dekhta hai ki yeh id pehle dekha gaya hai ya nahi. Dekha gaya hai toh fingerprint (content+channels+scheduledAt) match karke purana post return; nahi dekha toh naya record banta hai aur id register ho jaata hai.
in_this_project: src/scheduler.ts ke schedulePost() mein `const existingId = this.idempotency.get(clientRequestId)`. Test file test/schedule.test.ts ke describe("idempotent scheduling") block mein 'the same clientRequestId with the same content/channels/time returns the original, creates nothing new' isko directly prove karta hai.
advantages: Caller ko bina extra coordination ke safe retry milta hai
Server ko duplicate detect karne ke liye caller ki intent clearly pata chalti hai
Simple Map-based lookup, extra infra nahi chahiye
disadvantages: Caller ko khud ek meaningful unique id generate karna padta hai
Is project mein id kabhi expire nahi hota, memory grow karti hai
common_mistakes: Server-side random id generate karke 'idempotent' bol dena
clientRequestId ko content ke saath store na karna, sirf 'already seen' bool rakhna (phir conflict detect nahi hoga)

question: What is the difference between "scheduled" and "immediate" dispatch, and does this project support immediate dispatch?
answer_hinglish:
Scheduled dispatch matlab post ko ek FUTURE time par bhejna hai -- caller ek scheduledAt timestamp deta hai aur system khud decide karta hai kab bhejna hai, jab woh time aa jaaye. Immediate dispatch matlab request aate hi, bina kisi wait ke, turant bhej dena.

Is project mein sirf scheduled dispatch ka model hai, par ek trick se immediate bhi same mechanism se ho jaata hai: agar caller scheduledAt = clock.now() de de (yaani 'abhi'), tick() usse turant due maan lega as soon as woh call hota hai. Koi separate 'sendNow()' function nahi hai -- schedulePost() ke baad tick() call karna hi dispatch trigger karta hai, chahe scheduledAt future ho ya abhi ka time.

Yeh design decision important hai: ek hi code path (tick()) dono cases handle karta hai, do alag functions maintain nahi karne padte. Test 'dispatches exactly at scheduledAt (inclusive boundary)' isi ko prove karta hai -- scheduledAt == now bhi dispatch ho jaata hai, strictly less-than nahi chahiye.
why_needed: Real products mein user kabhi 'abhi post karo' chahta hai, kabhi 'kal subah 9 baje'. Ek hi scheduling primitive se dono serve karna code simpler rakhta hai.
real_world_analogy: Courier booking app mein ek hi form hota hai 'pickup time' field ke saath -- 'Now' bhi ek valid option hai, 'Tomorrow 9 AM' bhi. Backend ke liye dono same tarah ek scheduled pickup hi hain, sirf time alag hai.
how_it_works: schedulePost() scheduledAt ko sirf 'not in the past' check karta hai (>= clock.now()). tick() har pending channel ka nextAttemptAt <= now dekhta hai -- yeh check scheduledAt se seedha derive hota hai jab tak koi attempt nahi hua.
in_this_project: src/scheduler.ts mein requireFutureScheduledAt() aur tick()'s due filter `delivery.nextAttemptAt <= now`. test/tick.test.ts ka 'dispatches exactly at scheduledAt (inclusive boundary)' test.
advantages: Ek hi dispatch path, do APIs nahi maintain karne
scheduledAt == now ka inclusive boundary test se guaranteed hai
disadvantages: 'Immediate' sirf scheduledAt=now daalne se simulate hota hai, koi fast-path optimization nahi
common_mistakes: scheduledAt < now (exclusive) check karna, jisse scheduledAt=now reject ho jaayega
Immediate aur scheduled dispatch ke liye do alag functions banana jab zaroorat nahi
follow_up_questions: Why is the scheduledAt boundary inclusive rather than exclusive?
What would change if you wanted a true 'send right now, skip the queue' fast path?

question: What is retry with backoff, in simple terms, and why not just retry immediately after a failure?
answer_hinglish:
Retry with backoff ka matlab hai: ek attempt fail ho jaaye toh turant dobara try nahi karte, kuch WAIT karte hain, phir try karte hain. 'Backoff' isliye kyunki har fail ke baad wait time badhta jaata hai (exponential backoff).

Turant retry karna galat hai kyunki agar provider temporarily down hai (jaise mastodon instance down), turant dobara call karna sirf usi down system par aur load daalega, aur agar hazaaron posts ek saath fail ho rahe hain toh sab turant retry karenge -- yeh 'thundering herd' problem create karta hai. Thoda wait karne se provider ko recover hone ka time milta hai.

Is project mein backoff formula hai: initialBackoffMs * 2^(attempt-1), par ek max cap (maxBackoffMs) ke saath taaki wait time infinite na badhta rahe. Jaise initial 1 minute hai toh: attempt 1 fail -> 1 min wait, attempt 2 fail -> 2 min wait, attempt 3 fail -> 4 min wait... jab tak cap na lage.
why_needed: Bina backoff ke, ek down provider par repeated hammering hota hai -- na provider ko recover hone ka time milta hai, na scheduler ka resource bachta hai.
real_world_analogy: Jab koi phone nahi utha raha, tum turant 10 baar call nahi karte -- thodi der ruk kar try karte ho, phir thoda zyada ruk kar, taaki doosra bande ko bhi busy se free hone ka time mile.
how_it_works: dispatchChannel() mein failure par `delivery.nextAttemptAt = now + backoffMs(attempts, initialBackoffMs, maxBackoffMs)` set hota hai. tick() tab tak us channel ko touch nahi karta jab tak nextAttemptAt na aa jaaye.
in_this_project: src/scheduler.ts::backoffMs function: `Math.min(maxMs, initialMs * Math.pow(2, attempt - 1))`. test/tick.test.ts ka 'backoff grows between attempts (exponential)' aur 'respects the backoff delay' tests.
advantages: Temporarily-down providers ko recovery time milta hai
Thundering herd risk kam hota hai
Simple formula, easy to reason about and test with ManualClock
disadvantages: Koi jitter (randomness) nahi hai, isliye bahut saare channels agar same time par fail ho jaayen toh unka retry bhi same time par lineup ho sakta hai

Backoff formula khud retryable aur permanent failure mein fark nahi karta -- woh fark stage 2 mein dispatchChannel karta hai (`retryable: false` wali failure backoff schedule ko skip karke seedha dead_letter jaati hai), formula untouched rehta hai
common_mistakes: Backoff cap bhool jaana, jisse wait time practically infinite ho jaata hai
Backoff ko real setTimeout se implement karna instead of a checked nextAttemptAt + Clock
follow_up_questions: What is jitter and why might you add it to this formula?
What happens to nextAttemptAt once a channel reaches dead_letter?
How would you test exponential growth without waiting in real time?

question: What does "dead-lettering" a channel mean here, and what happens to it afterwards?
answer_hinglish:
Dead-lettering matlab system ne us channel ko permanently "give up" kar diya. Do raaste hain wahan tak pahunchne ke: (1) channel ne apne saare allowed attempts use kar liye (maxAttempts baar try kiya) aur har baar fail hua, ya (2) stage 2 se, provider ne failure ko PERMANENT bola (`retryable: false`, jaise account disconnected) -- tab channel usi attempt par dead-letter ho jaata hai, chahe attempt 1 hi kyun na ho. Status 'dead_letter' ban jaata hai, aur yeh TERMINAL hai: iske baad koi bhi tick() call, chahe clock kitna hi aage advance ho, us channel ko kabhi dobara try nahi karega.

Dead letter ka matlab data khona nahi hai -- delivery record apni jagah rehta hai, uska lastError (kyun fail hua) aur attempts count (kitni baar try hua) store rehte hain diagnostics ke liye. Bas ab provider.send() dobara call nahi hoga us (post, channel) combination ke liye.

Yeh crucial hai kyunki agar dead-lettered channel ko har tick() phir se try karta rahe, woh resources waste karega ek aisi cheez par jo kabhi succeed nahi hogi (ordinary failure attempts khatam hone tak retry hoti hai, permanent failure ko retry hi nahi kiya jaata -- dono ka end state same 'dead_letter' hai).
why_needed: Bina dead-letter ke, ek permanently-broken channel har tick() call par provider ko call karta rahega forever, resources waste karte hue aur kabhi result nahi milega.
real_world_analogy: Courier ne ek address par 5 baar delivery try ki, ghar par koi nahi mila -- ab woh parcel ko 'undeliverable' mark kar depot bhej deta hai, baar baar wahi address try nahi karta.
how_it_works: dispatchChannel() mein failure ke baad check hota hai `const permanent = result.retryable === false; if (permanent || delivery.attempts >= delivery.maxAttempts) delivery.status = "dead_letter"`, warna backoff ke saath nextAttemptAt set hota hai.
in_this_project: src/scheduler.ts::dispatchChannel. test/tick.test.ts ka 'exhausting maxAttempts moves the channel to dead_letter and it is never retried again' -- yeh provider call count check karke prove karta hai ki aage koi call nahi hoti. Stage 2 ka 'permanent failures (retryable: false)' describe block ka 'dead-letters on the very first attempt, skipping the retry schedule entirely' test permanent path prove karta hai (attempts 1, maxAttempts 5 hone ke bawajood).
advantages: Permanently-broken channel resources waste nahi karta
lastError aur attempts diagnostics ke liye preserved rehte hain
disadvantages: Ek baar dead_letter hone ke baad koi automatic recovery nahi -- caller ko khud dekhna padega aur naya action lena padega
dead_letter record khud yeh field nahi rakhta ki give-up permanent failure ki wajah se hua ya maxAttempts exhaust hone se -- `lastError` aur `attempts < maxAttempts` se infer karna padta hai
common_mistakes: Dead-lettered channel ko silently retry karte rehna
dead_letter hone par delivery record delete kar dena (diagnostics kho jaate hain)

question: What is the Strategy pattern intuition behind FakeChannelProvider, and why is a channel just a string key?
answer_hinglish:
Strategy pattern ka seedha idea hai: ek common interface ho, aur alag alag implementations usse fulfill karen -- caller sirf interface ke saath kaam kare, implementation detail se matlab na ho. Yahan FakeChannelProvider ek interface hai jiska ek method hai send(). AlwaysSucceedsProvider, AlwaysFailsProvider aur FlakyProvider teen alag 'strategies' hain jo yeh interface implement karti hain.

Scheduler ko sirf yeh pata hai ki 'linkedin' naam ke channel ke piche kuch hai jo FakeChannelProvider interface follow karta hai -- scheduler ko kabhi yeh nahi pata ki 'linkedin' actually kya karta hai, real API hai ya fake, succeed karega ya fail. Isliye channel ek plain string key hai providers map mein, koi closed enum nahi (jaise `type Channel = "linkedin" | "twitter"`).

Yeh design testing ko bahut easy banata hai: test mein kisi bhi channel ke piche FlakyProvider daal sakte ho retry logic test karne ke liye, production mein wahi key ke piche kal ek real LinkedIn API wrapper daal sakte ho -- scheduler ka code ek line bhi nahi badlega.
why_needed: Agar scheduler khud har platform ke API details jaanta, naya channel add karne ke liye scheduler ka code hi badalna padta. Strategy se naya channel = bas ek nayi provider class register karo.
real_world_analogy: Payment gateway integration jaisa -- checkout page ko nahi pata ki payment Stripe se ho raha hai ya Razorpay se, woh sirf ek common 'charge()' interface call karta hai. Nayi payment method add karne ke liye checkout page ka code nahi badalta.
how_it_works: SchedulerOptions.providers ek `Record<string, FakeChannelProvider>` hai. schedulePost() channel string ko is map mein lookup karta hai (UNKNOWN_CHANNEL agar nahi mila), dispatchChannel() usi map se provider nikal kar `.send()` call karta hai.
in_this_project: src/providers.ts ka FakeChannelProvider interface aur teen implementations. src/scheduler.ts constructor mein `this.providers = options.providers`. demo.ts mein chaar channels register hote hain: linkedin/twitter/mastodon/instagram (instagram ek `new AlwaysFailsProvider("account disconnected", false)` hai, stage 2 ka permanent failure), saare sirf string keys hain.
advantages: Naya channel add karna sirf ek nayi provider class, scheduler code untouched
Testing mein har behaviour (succeeds/fails/flaky) ko ek fake se simulate karna easy
disadvantages: String key hone se typo se galat channel name easily ban sakta hai (runtime par UNKNOWN_CHANNEL se pakda jaata hai, compile time par nahi)
common_mistakes: Channel ko closed enum banana, jisse naye channel ke liye scheduler ka type hi badalna pade
Scheduler ke andar platform-specific logic (jaise 'if channel === twitter') likhna
follow_up_questions: What happens if schedulePost is called with a channel key that has no registered provider?
Why does FakeChannelProvider only have one method?
How would you add a real LinkedIn integration without touching SocialScheduler?

question: Why does this project never call a real social media API, and what does that trade off against?
answer_hinglish:
Yeh project bilkul is repo ke 21-notification aur 22-messaging ki philosophy follow karta hai: fake providers only, koi real network call kabhi nahi hota. AlwaysSucceedsProvider, AlwaysFailsProvider aur FlakyProvider sab in-memory hain, instantly resolve karte hain (ya test mein manually resolve hote hain).

Iska fayda yeh hai ki tests 100% deterministic aur fast hain -- koi real LinkedIn ya Twitter API down ho ya rate-limit kare, tests isse unaffected rehte hain. Pure clock control (ManualClock) se backoff/due-detection ke boundaries exactly test ho paate hain bina real sleep ke.

Trade-off yeh hai ki yeh project OAuth, real rate limits, real API error shapes (jaise Twitter ka 429 rate-limit response), ya real network latency/timeouts handle nahi karta -- woh sab 'real provider integration' banate waqt add karna padega, fake provider ki jagah. FakeChannelProvider interface ko hi ek real implementation se replace karna hoga, scheduler logic same rahega.
why_needed: Real APIs par dependency hone se tests flaky, slow aur external outage se affected ho jaate. Fake providers isolate karte hain ki hum KYA test kar rahe hain -- scheduler ka logic, na ki kisi third-party platform ka uptime.
real_world_analogy: Pilot training simulator mein real plane nahi uraate -- simulator mein hi engine fail jaisi situations practice karte hain, bina real risk ke, aur jab chaho exact same scenario dobara trigger kar sakte ho.
how_it_works: Scheduler sirf FakeChannelProvider interface se baat karta hai; koi HTTP client, koi fetch(), koi SDK import nahi hai is codebase mein.
in_this_project: README.md ki line: 'There are no real providers: nothing in this project ever sends a real post over a network.' PLAN.md 'Not in scope' section mein 'Real social platform APIs (and OAuth to them)' explicitly listed hai.
advantages: Deterministic, fast tests
Koi external outage test suite ko affect nahi karta
Clock injection se exact timing boundaries test hote hain
disadvantages: Real-world API quirks (rate limits, auth errors, partial outages ka exact shape) simulate nahi hote
OAuth, credential refresh jaisa kuch bhi implement nahi hai
common_mistakes: Fake providers ko bhool kar yeh sochna ki project production-ready hai
Real API integration karte waqt FakeChannelProvider interface ko hi todna, jab usse implement karna kaafi hota

What would a real provider's error handling need that a fake one doesn't?

question: In plain terms, walk through what happens from schedulePost() to a channel showing status 'sent' -- the full basic lifecycle.
answer_hinglish:
Step by step: (1) Caller schedulePost({clientRequestId, content, channels, scheduledAt}) call karta hai. (2) Validation hoti hai -- content, channels ki shape, scheduledAt future mein hai ya nahi. (3) Idempotency check -- naya request hai toh aage badhte hain. (4) Har channel ke liye ek ChannelDelivery banta hai, status='pending', attempts=0, nextAttemptAt=scheduledAt. (5) Post store ho jaata hai, function return ho jaata hai -- abhi tak kuch bhi 'bheja' nahi gaya.

(6) Baad mein, kisi bhi waqt, caller tick() call karta hai. (7) tick() dekhta hai konse channels due hain (nextAttemptAt <= abhi ka time) aur pending hain. (8) Due channel ke liye dispatchChannel() chalta hai: attempts++ hota hai, phir provider.send() await hota hai. (9) Agar provider 'sent' return kare, delivery.status='sent' ban jaata hai, providerId aur sentAt record hote hain -- yeh terminal hai, ab kabhi touch nahi hoga.

Important baat: schedule karna aur dispatch karna do alag steps hain -- schedulePost() kabhi provider ko call nahi karta, sirf tick() karta hai. Yeh separation hi scheduling ko possible banata hai.
why_needed: Beginner interview mein yeh basic flow clearly bolna zaroori hai -- interviewer dekhna chahta hai ki candidate ko pata hai scheduling aur dispatching alag concerns hain.
real_world_analogy: Ek letter likh kar postbox mein daalna (schedule) aur postman ka use ake pick up karna (dispatch) do alag events hain -- letter postbox mein pada rehta hai jab tak postman apna round na le.
how_it_works: schedulePost() sirf state create karta hai; tick() hi actual provider.send() call karta hai, jab bhi caller usse invoke kare.
in_this_project: README.md ka Usage code block exactly yeh sequence dikhata hai: schedulePost() call, phir clock.advance(), phir await scheduler.tick().
advantages: Scheduling aur dispatch decoupled, easy to reason about and test separately
disadvantages: Caller ko khud tick() call karte rehna padta hai; koi internal timer nahi hai
common_mistakes: Yeh sochna ki schedulePost() khud provider ko call karta hai
tick() ko bhool jaana aur assume karna ki scheduledAt hit hote hi automatically send ho jaayega

question: Why is there one ChannelDelivery per channel instead of one status field on the whole post?
answer_hinglish:
Agar poore post par ek hi status hota, toh ek post jo 3 channels target kar raha hai, uska 'overall status' kya hoga jab linkedin sent ho gaya ho par twitter abhi retry kar raha ho aur mastodon dead-letter ho gaya ho? Koi bhi single value (sent/failed/partial) poori information nahi de sakta -- 'delivered' asal mein ek (post, channel) PAIR ki property hai, sirf post ki nahi.

Isliye yahan ek post ke andar `deliveries: Record<string, ChannelDelivery>` hota hai -- har channel ki apni independent copy: apna status, apna attempts count, apna nextAttemptAt, apna lastError. Ek channel ka fail hona ya retry karna doosre channel ke kisi bhi field ko touch nahi karta.

Yeh exactly project 22 (messaging) ke per-recipient receipt map jaisa reasoning hai -- wahan ek message ka 'delivered' status har recipient ke liye alag track hota hai, kyunki ek recipient online hai aur dusra offline, dono ka result alag hoga. Yahan channel recipient ki jagah lete hain.
why_needed: Multi-channel fan-out mein har target independently succeed ya fail kar sakta hai. Single post-level status information loss karega aur galat UI/alerts create karega.
real_world_analogy: Ek hi shaadi ka invitation 3 relatives ko bheja -- ek ne turant accept kiya, dusra abhi tak reply nahi kiya (follow up chal raha hai), teesra available hi nahi mila. Teeno ka status alag track hoga, ek hi 'invitation status' nahi bata sakta sabka haal.
how_it_works: schedulePost() har channel ke liye alag ChannelDelivery object banata hai, channel name se keyed. Koi dusra channel object ka reference share nahi karta.
in_this_project: src/types.ts::ChannelDelivery aur ScheduledPost.deliveries. Test 'fans out one independent delivery per channel' (test/schedule.test.ts) directly check karta hai `post.deliveries.linkedin !== post.deliveries.twitter`.
advantages: Har channel ka result accurately represent hota hai
Ek channel ki retries doosre channel ke counters ko corrupt nahi kar sakti
disadvantages: Caller ko 'overall post status' chahiye toh usse khud N deliveries ko aggregate karna padega
common_mistakes: Post par single status field rakhna aur 'worst of N channels' jaisi logic baad mein hack karna
Deliveries ko ek shared mutable object se banana (reference accidentally share ho jaana)

question: Why is there no separate 'failed' status next to pending/sent/dead_letter/canceled?
answer_hinglish:
Is project ka status enum sirf 4 values rakhta hai: pending, sent, dead_letter, canceled. Ek 'failed' status deliberately NAHI hai, jabki kaafi designs mein log karte hain. Wajah: ek failed attempt jiske paas abhi retries baaki hain, woh sirf 'pending' rehta hai -- woh apne next attempt ka WAIT kar raha hai, exactly waise hi jaise apne first attempt se pehle wait kar raha tha.

Agar ek alag 'failed' status hota (jo phir 'pending' mein wapas transition ho jaata jab retry due ho), yeh sirf 'pending' kehne ka doosra tareeka hota -- koi nayi information nahi deta, bas ek extra field/transition add karta jisko sync mein rakhna padta. Is repo ka rule hai: 'a status field with guarded transitions is enough' -- do fields jo agree karne chahiye (status + will-retry flag) se better hai ek single field jiske transitions clearly guarded hain.

Sirf jab attempts maxAttempts tak exhaust ho jaate hain, ya (stage 2 se) provider failure ko `retryable: false` bolta hai, TABHI yeh terminal 'dead_letter' banta hai -- yahi asli 'give up' moment hai, '`failed`' nahi. Dhyan do, stage 2 ne bhi koi naya status add nahi kiya -- permanent failure bhi same 'dead_letter' mein jaati hai.
why_needed: Do states jo same meaning carry karte hain (pending vs transient-failed) bugs ka source ban sakte hain jab unka sync galat ho jaaye. Ek clean enum simpler aur bug-resistant hai.
real_world_analogy: Doctor ka appointment 'rescheduled' hai -- usse 'cancelled' mark karna galat hoga, woh sirf apna NEXT slot wait kar raha hai, same as pehle wala slot wait kar raha tha.
how_it_works: dispatchChannel() mein failure case: `if (permanent || attempts >= maxAttempts) status = 'dead_letter'; else nextAttemptAt = now + backoff` (permanent = `result.retryable === false`, stage 2) -- status khud 'pending' hi rehta hai dusre case mein.
in_this_project: src/types.ts::ChannelStatus = "pending" | "sent" | "dead_letter" | "canceled". PLAN.md ka 'One status enum per channel, not two' decision section exactly yeh reasoning likhta hai.
code_example:
// real, src/types.ts
export type ChannelStatus = "pending" | "sent" | "dead_letter" | "canceled";
advantages: Ek hi field, no sync-between-two-fields bugs
Fewer states to test and reason about
disadvantages: Caller ko turant yeh pata nahi chalta ki ek channel 'just failed once' hai ya 'never even tried' -- dono pending hain (attempts field se dekhna padega)
common_mistakes: Ek 'failed' transient status add karna aur phir usse manually 'pending' mein wapas convert karna
attempts count ko status ke saath confuse karna

question: How does the clientRequestId idempotency scheme distinguish a replay from a conflict?
answer_hinglish:
Jab schedulePost() same clientRequestId dusri baar dekhta hai, woh ek fingerprint compare karta hai -- fingerprint content + sorted-unique channels + scheduledAt se bana hota hai. Agar naya request ka fingerprint PURANE post ke stored fingerprint se match karta hai, yeh ek REPLAY hai -- original post return ho jaata hai, kuch naya nahi banta.

Agar fingerprint match nahi karta (matlab same id, par content ya channels ya scheduledAt mein se koi alag hai), yeh ek CONFLICT hai -- IDEMPOTENCY_CONFLICT error throw hota hai, aur original post bilkul untouched rehta hai. Yeh important hai: ek buggy client jo galti se same id reuse kar de ek different request ke liye, use silently overwrite nahi hone dena.

Interesting detail: fingerprint compute karne ke liye bhi basic shape validation (requireContent, requireChannelsShape, requireScheduledAtShape) chalti hai -- par channel KNOWN hai ya nahi, yeh check REPLAY path mein nahi hota, kyunki replay ek request jo pehle hi accepted thi usko dobara validate nahi karta.
why_needed: Replay aur conflict dono 'same id dekha gaya' cases hain, par unka correct behaviour bilkul alag hona chahiye -- replay safe honi chahiye, conflict loudly fail honi chahiye.
real_world_analogy: Ek hi tracking number do baar deke dekha -- agar dono baar same parcel details hain, system bolta hai 'haan yeh wahi parcel hai'. Par agar tracking number same hai par parcel ka weight/address alag hai, system bolega 'yeh number already kisi doosre parcel ke liye use ho chuka hai'.
how_it_works: fingerprintOf(content, channels, scheduledAt) = JSON.stringify({content, channels: [...new Set(channels)].sort(), scheduledAt}). Comparison existing.fingerprint se hota hai.
in_this_project: src/scheduler.ts::fingerprintOf aur schedulePost() ka idempotency branch. Tests: 'the same clientRequestId with different content is a conflict and creates nothing new', 'channel order does not matter for the replay match'.
advantages: Ek hi check se replay aur conflict dono detect ho jaate hain
Channel order independence se caller ko array ordering ki chinta nahi karni padti
disadvantages: Fingerprint JSON.stringify use karta hai -- koi field jo serialization order se affected ho sakta hai, theoretically issue de sakta hai (yahan sirf primitives/sorted array hone se safe hai)

question: Why is tick() a polling model instead of being driven by real timers per post?
answer_hinglish:
tick() ek POLL hai -- caller usse kabhi bhi, kisi bhi interval par call kar sakta hai, aur tick() har call par saare posts scan karta hai dekhne ke liye konse channels due hain. Ek real-timer design iska opposite hota -- har post ke liye ek setTimeout(ya cron entry) schedule hota jo exactly scheduledAt par fire ho.

Polling choose kiya gaya kyunki yeh Clock abstraction ke saath perfectly fit karta hai -- tests ManualClock.advance() karke, bina real time wait kiye, exact boundaries check kar sakte hain. Real per-post timers ko test karna much harder hota (real setTimeout ya fake-timer libraries ki zaroorat), aur agar process crash ho jaaye, timers ka state khona easy hota hai.

Trade-off: dispatch ki actual latency poll interval par depend karti hai -- agar caller tick() ko 1 minute mein ek baar call kare, ek due post ko up to 1 minute ki delay ho sakti hai dispatch hone mein. Yeh exactly project 21's flushDue() jaisa hi trade-off hai.
why_needed: Polling model se testing deterministic ho jaati hai (Clock control) aur caller ko full control milta hai dispatch ki frequency par, bina internal timer infrastructure maintain kiye.
real_world_analogy: Postman ek fixed route par din mein kuch baar aata hai aur dekh ke jaata hai koi letter ready hai ya nahi -- har ghar ke liye alag se koi bell nahi bajti jab unka letter ready ho.
how_it_works: tick() posts.values() ke saath saare deliveries ko scan karta hai, `nextAttemptAt <= now` aur status='pending' wale ko 'due' maan kar dispatch karta hai.
in_this_project: src/scheduler.ts::tick. demo.ts mein caller manually `await scheduler.tick()` multiple baar call karta hai clock.advance() ke beech mein.

Koi per-post timer infrastructure maintain nahi karni padti
Caller ko dispatch frequency par full control
disadvantages: Dispatch latency poll interval se bound hai
Har tick() full scan karta hai (O(total deliveries)), bade scale par inefficient
common_mistakes: Yeh assume karna ki scheduledAt hit hote hi automatically dispatch ho jaayega
tick() ko bahut rarely call karna aur latency ki shikayat karna

question: Walk through the exact exponential backoff formula and how the cap works.
answer_hinglish:
Formula hai: `backoffMs(attempt) = min(maxBackoffMs, initialBackoffMs * 2^(attempt-1))`. Attempt yahan woh number hai jo just fail hua -- attempt 1 fail hua toh wait = initialBackoffMs * 2^0 = initialBackoffMs. Attempt 2 fail hua toh wait = initialBackoffMs * 2^1 = 2x. Attempt 3 fail hua toh 4x, aur aise hi doubling hoti hai.

maxBackoffMs ek upper cap hai -- jaise hi calculated value is cap se badi ho jaaye, wait time cap par fix ho jaata hai, aur badhta nahi. Isse wait time practically infinite hone se bachta hai (jaise agar maxAttempts bahut zyada ho aur initial backoff bhi bada ho, exponential growth bahut fast real-world-unreasonable numbers tak pahunch jaata).

constructor mein validation hai ki maxBackoffMs >= initialBackoffMs hamesha ho (warna cap formula hi galat behave karega) -- yeh K3 mutation check se verify hua hai. Test 'backoff is capped at maxBackoffMs' exactly yeh prove karta hai, successive attempts ke delay ko maxBackoffMs se compare karke.
why_needed: Pure exponential growth bina cap ke kuch attempts ke baad hours/days tak wait time pohocha dega -- jo kisi bhi practical retry policy ke liye bekaar hai. Cap ensures wait time ek reasonable bound ke andar rehta hai.
real_world_analogy: Network protocols (jaise TCP) mein bhi retransmission timeout exponentially badhta hai har retry par, par kisi max value tak hi, uske baad flat reh jaata hai.
how_it_works: dispatchChannel() failure branch mein: `delivery.nextAttemptAt = now + backoffMs(delivery.attempts, this.initialBackoffMs, this.maxBackoffMs)`.
in_this_project: src/scheduler.ts::backoffMs function aur constructor's K3 validation `maxBackoffMs >= initialBackoffMs`. test/tick.test.ts ka 'backoff grows between attempts (exponential)' aur 'backoff is capped at maxBackoffMs'.
advantages: Growth exponential, lekin practically bound by the cap
Simple pure function, easy to unit test independent of the scheduler
disadvantages: No jitter -- many channels failing at once could all retry at similarly-spaced times
common_mistakes: attempt ko 0-indexed treat karna formula mein (yahan attempt 1-indexed hai, 2^(attempt-1))
Cap ko backoffMs() ke andar na laga kar bahar galat jagah apply karna

question: Why does editPost need to be stricter than cancelChannel/cancelPost -- what is the key difference in what each operation is undoing?
answer_hinglish:
cancelChannel/cancelPost ek simple 'still pending' rule use karte hain -- koi channel jo abhi tak terminal nahi hua (sent/dead_letter/canceled nahi hai), usse cancel kiya ja sakta hai, chahe woh mid-retry ho (attempts > 0, par status abhi bhi pending). Cancel karne mein kuch 'undo' nahi karna -- sirf ek FUTURE attempt ko hone se rokna hai, jo provider call kabhi start hi nahi hua use start hone se rokna hai.

editPost zyada strict hai: content POST ka ek field hai, per-channel nahi. Agar koi bhi channel already ek attempt dekh chuka hai (chahe woh attempt fail hua ho aur abhi retry ka wait kar raha ho), provider ne already PURANA content dekh liya hai -- us attempt ko 'un-see' nahi kiya ja sakta. Agar edit allow kar diya jaaye, kuch channels purana content dikhayenge, kuch naya -- aur system mein koi tarika nahi hai yeh express karne ka ki ek post 'half-edited' hai.

Yeh asymmetry PLAN.md mein explicitly documented hai -- dono rules 'only while still pending' hi hain literal sense mein, par editPost is rule ki STRICTER reading leta hai (zero attempts on every non-canceled channel), jabki cancel sirf 'abhi terminal nahi hua' check karta hai.
why_needed: Cancel aur edit bilkul alag guarantees deti hain -- cancel sirf future ko rokta hai, edit past ko bhi effectively rewrite karne ki koshish karta hai jo content ke liye possible nahi hai once a provider has seen it.
real_world_analogy: Ek courier ko cancel karna -- agar woh abhi nikla hi nahi hai, cancel kar sakte ho. Par uska content (jo letter mein likha hai) badalna -- agar courier already ek baar try kar chuka hai (chahe deliver na hua ho), woh uska content already dekh chuka hai, usse 'unsee' nahi kar sakte.
how_it_works: editPost() loop karta hai har non-canceled delivery par aur check karta hai `attempts > 0` -- agar kisi ek ka bhi attempts > 0 hai, poora POST_ALREADY_DISPATCHED se reject ho jaata hai. cancelChannel/cancelPost sirf `status !== pending` check karte hain.
in_this_project: src/scheduler.ts::editPost ka loop `if (delivery.status === "canceled") continue; if (delivery.attempts > 0) throw POST_ALREADY_DISPATCHED`. test/cancel-edit.test.ts ka 'rejects editing a post once ANY channel has been attempted, even if that channel is still pending (mid-retry)' aur 'allows editing a post whose only channel was canceled AFTER an attempt (mid-retry cancel)'.
advantages: Content consistency guaranteed -- never a half-edited post across channels
Cancel stays simple and permissive since it never needs to undo anything already seen
disadvantages: Ek single flaky retry caller ke liye poore post ka edit lock kar deta hai, chahe woh channel abhi bhi pending ho
common_mistakes: editPost ko cancelChannel jaisa 'still pending' rule se implement karna (E3 mutation gap exactly yahi test karta hai)
Canceled channels ko bhi attempts>0 check mein include karna, jisse valid edits bhi reject ho jaayen

question: If schedulePost() ever needed to await something (say, a database write) before committing, what would break in the current idempotency scheme and how would you fix it?
answer_hinglish:
Abhi schedulePost() poora SYNCHRONOUS hai -- validate, build, store, sab ek hi JavaScript turn mein hota hai, koi await nahi. Isi liye ek plain 'check the map, then set it' (idempotency.get() phir idempotency.set()) already safe hai: JavaScript function body ko ek atomic turn mein chalata hai, toh dusri call sirf pehli ke return hone ke BAAD hi start ho sakti hai.

Agar koi REAL await add ho jaaye commit se pehle (jaise `await db.insert(post)`), yeh guarantee toot jaati hai. Do concurrent calls same clientRequestId ke saath, dono idempotency.get() karenge, dono 'not found' dekhenge (kyunki koi abhi set nahi hua), dono DB insert shuru kar denge -- result: do posts ban jaayenge ek hi clientRequestId ke liye.

Fix: ek SYNCHRONOUS placeholder claim karna commit se pehle -- jaise is project ka contrasting case, project 22 (messaging) ka pendingOps map. Pehle synchronously `pendingOps.set(clientRequestId, PLACEHOLDER)` karo (yeh abhi bhi synchronous hai, race-safe), PHIR await karo DB write ke liye, aur result se placeholder ko real postId se replace karo. Agar dusri call beech mein aaye, use placeholder dikhega aur woh wait karegi ya conflict throw karegi, na ki apna naya insert start karegi.
why_needed: Concurrency correctness sirf 'map lookup use karna' se nahi aati -- yeh depend karta hai ki check-then-set atomic hai ya nahi. Ek real await beech mein aane se atomicity toot jaati hai agar claim pehle na li jaaye.
real_world_analogy: Restaurant mein table booking: agar waiter pehle check kare 'table free hai?' phir jaake kisi ko bulane jaaye (delay), beech mein doosra waiter bhi wahi table dusre customer ko de sakta hai. Isliye turant 'reserved' tag laga dena chahiye check karte hi, bulaane jaane se pehle.
how_it_works: Ek synchronous claim pehle `pendingOps.set(clientRequestId, PLACEHOLDER)` karti hai (abhi bhi ek synchronous Map write hai, safe hai), phir await hota hai, phir result se placeholder ko real value se replace kiya jaata hai -- isi tarah project 22's messenger.ts apna IdempotencyEntry claim karta hai await se pehle.
in_this_project: Yeh abhi is project mein HAPPEN nahi karta -- schedulePost() mein koi await hi nahi hai. PLAN.md explicitly contrast karta hai: 'Unlike project 22 (messaging) stage 2, where a REAL await before the commit meant a plain map lookup could not dedupe truly concurrent duplicates and a synchronous claim was required'.
common_mistakes: Ek await add kar dena bina synchronous claim ke, yeh sochte hue ki Map lookup hamesha safe hai
Placeholder ko commit se PEHLE claim na karna, uske baad claim karna (race window khula reh jaata hai)
follow_up_questions: How does project 22's messenger.ts actually implement this placeholder claim?
What should happen to a caller that sees a placeholder it didn't create?
Would this change affect tick(), which already has an await?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Synchronous claim ek extra Map entry aur ek extra state (pending/resolved) maintain karne ki cost leti hai, par woh cost race-safety ke against justified hai jab bhi commit path mein ek real await ho. Plain check-then-set sirf tab tak safe hai jab tak pura commit path synchronous ho.
advanced.failure_scenarios: Agar DB write fail ho jaaye claim lene ke baad, placeholder ko explicitly rollback/delete karna padega, warna woh clientRequestId permanently stuck reh jaayega 'in progress' state mein -- yeh ek naya failure mode hai jo pure-synchronous design mein exist hi nahi karta.
advanced.alternatives: Database-level unique constraint (clientRequestId par UNIQUE index) ek alternative hai -- dono concurrent inserts try karenge, ek succeed karega, dusra constraint-violation error dega jisse caller conflict/replay resolve kar sake, bina application-level placeholder ke.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: Zyada concurrent callers ke saath, in-memory placeholder map single process tak limited rahega -- multiple server instances ke across idempotency ke liye yeh claim shared storage (Redis SETNX, ya DB unique constraint) mein move karna padega.
advanced.production_improvements: Production mein distributed lock (Redis SETNX with TTL) ya DB unique constraint + retry-on-conflict pattern use karte, taaki claim bhi crash-safe ho (process crash hone par stuck placeholder na reh jaaye).

question: What is the exact validation order inside schedulePost(), and why does the idempotency check sit where it does?
answer_hinglish:
Order important hai kyunki 'an error means nothing happened' rule follow karna hai, aur replay ko original request se differently treat karna hai. Exact order: (1) requireClientRequestId -- shape check (non-empty string, length limit), yeh check REPLAY ya nahi, dono case mein hona chahiye kyunki ek malformed id kabhi valid nahi hota. (2) idempotency map mein lookup -- agar id already dekha gaya hai, fingerprint compute karo (requireContent/requireChannelsShape/requireScheduledAtShape se, SHAPE-only checks) aur compare karo: match toh existing return, mismatch toh IDEMPOTENCY_CONFLICT.

(3) Agar naya request hai (id pehli baar), DEEPER semantic checks chalte hain: requireContent (length), requireValidChannels (channel registered hai ya nahi -- UNKNOWN_CHANNEL), requireFutureScheduledAt (SCHEDULED_AT_IN_PAST). (4) Sab pass hone ke baad hi state banta hai aur store hota hai.

Kyun yeh order matter karta hai: shape checks (clientRequestId, content format, channels array shape, scheduledAt format) replay path mein BHI chalte hain kyunki fingerprint compute karne ke liye data ki shape jaanna zaroori hai -- par UNKNOWN_CHANNEL aur SCHEDULED_AT_IN_PAST jaise DEEPER checks replay mein nahi chalte, kyunki 'yeh request pehle VALID thi' already pata hai -- usse dobara validate karna galat hoga (ho sakta hai ab clock aage badh gaya ho aur scheduledAt 'past' lag raha ho, par woh pehle valid tha).
why_needed: Replay ko re-validate karna galat hai -- ek valid-pehle-accepted request ko later deeper check se reject karna inconsistent behaviour hai. Par malformed clientRequestId hamesha reject hona chahiye, replay ho ya na ho.
real_world_analogy: Jab tum ek purani entry ticket dikhate ho dobara entry ke liye, guard sirf dekhta hai 'yeh ticket genuine hai?' (shape check) -- woh dobara nahi check karta ki event abhi bhi chal raha hai ya nahi (deeper check), kyunki ticket pehle hi valid tha jab issue hua.
how_it_works: schedulePost() method body literally is order mein likha hai -- requireClientRequestId sabse pehle, phir idempotency.get(), phir agar replay to shape-only checks for fingerprint, phir agar naya to deep checks.
in_this_project: src/scheduler.ts::schedulePost ka comment block: 'The idempotency check itself runs AFTER the cheap shape checks ... BEFORE the deeper semantic checks'. requireChannelsShape vs requireValidChannels do alag functions hona isi separation ko dikhata hai.
advantages: Replay path never re-runs checks that could legitimately differ over time (like 'is this still in the future')
Malformed clientRequestId always rejected first, consistent behaviour
disadvantages: Two separate 'shape' vs 'valid' functions for channels adds a bit of indirection to follow
common_mistakes: Running UNKNOWN_CHANNEL or SCHEDULED_AT_IN_PAST checks on the replay path too, breaking replay semantics
Checking idempotency before even validating clientRequestId's own shape

question: How exactly does the idempotency map get checked and then set, and why is a plain check-then-set safe here?
answer_hinglish:
Code level par yeh simple hai: `const existingId = this.idempotency.get(clientRequestId)` (check), aur agar naya request hai, end mein `this.idempotency.set(clientRequestId, record.id)` (set). Dono ke beech koi await nahi hai -- saara validation, record build karna, posts.set() karna, sab synchronous JavaScript statements hain, ek ke baad ek, bina kisi microtask gap ke.

JavaScript single-threaded hai aur ek async function ka synchronous portion ek hi 'turn' mein poora chal jaata hai jab tak koi await na mile. Toh agar schedulePost() do baar synchronously call ho (ya ek ke baad ek, bina await ke beech mein), DUSRI call pehli call ke COMPLETE return hone ke baad hi start hoti hai -- is beech koi third call interleave nahi kar sakti.

Isliye plain 'check the map, then set it' safe hai: by the time dusri call idempotency.get() karti hai, pehli call ka idempotency.set() already ho chuka hota hai (agar pehli call pehle shuru hui thi). Yeh guarantee TABHI tak hold karti hai jab tak schedulePost() ke andar koi await na ho -- isi liye yeh ek deliberate decision hai, accident nahi.
why_needed: Concurrent-looking calls ko bhi safely dedupe karne ke liye yeh samajhna zaroori hai ki JavaScript ka synchronous execution model hi yahan safety provide kar raha hai, koi explicit lock nahi.
real_world_analogy: Ek single clerk ek counter par baitha hai, ek time par ek hi customer ko serve karta hai poora transaction complete karke -- agar transaction beech mein kabhi rukta nahi (no 'please wait, I'll call someone' step), doosra customer line mein peeche hi khada rahega jab tak pehla poora na ho jaaye.
how_it_works: idempotency ek `Map<string, string>` hai (clientRequestId -> postId). get() aur set() dono O(1) synchronous Map operations hain, beech mein koi Promise/await nahi.
in_this_project: src/scheduler.ts constructor mein `private readonly idempotency = new Map<string, string>()`. schedulePost() method ke top comment: 'tick() is the only place this project ever awaits anything ... and tick() is not on the scheduling path at all.'
advantages: No lock, no extra claim structure needed -- the language's own execution model gives safety
Simpler code than a claim-based scheme
disadvantages: This safety is fragile: adding even one await anywhere in schedulePost() before the Map.set() breaks it silently
common_mistakes: Assuming 'it's just a Map, so it must be thread-safe' without understanding WHY the synchronous path makes it safe here
Adding an await (e.g. for logging or a DB call) without reconsidering this safety argument

question: Walk through dispatchChannel()'s one await line by line -- what happens right before it, during it, and right after.
answer_hinglish:
dispatchChannel() ka poora method ek try/finally ke andar hai. RIGHT BEFORE the await: `delivery.attempts += 1` -- yeh SYNCHRONOUSLY hota hai, await se pehle hi. Yeh important hai kyunki is wajah se editPost() ek in-flight send ko detect kar sakta hai bina kisi extra guard ke -- attempts already incremented dikh jaata hai turant.

DURING the await: `result = await provider.send({postId, channel, content, attempt})`. Yeh ek inner try/catch ke andar hai -- agar provider throw kare, catch block usse `{ status: "failed", reason: "provider threw: ..." }` mein convert kar deta hai, poora function crash nahi hota aur Promise.all ka doosra channel affected nahi hota.

RIGHT AFTER the await: `const now = this.clock.now()` -- naya timestamp liya jaata hai (await ke baad time aage badh sakta hai, is wajah se dobara clock.now() call hota hai, pehle wala stale ho sakta hai). Phir result.status check hota hai: 'sent' par status/providerId/sentAt set hote hain; 'failed' par lastError set hota hai aur dead_letter ya nextAttemptAt decide hota hai. FINALLY block mein `this.dispatching.delete(key)` hamesha chalta hai, chahe kuch bhi ho (success, failure, ya koi aur crash) -- yeh guarantee karta hai ki guard kabhi 'stuck' nahi rehta.
why_needed: Yeh exact sequence (increment before await, try/catch around await, finally for cleanup) hi woh teen guarantees deta hai jo poora project rely karta hai: in-flight detection, throw-safety, aur guard cleanup.
real_world_analogy: Ek clerk kisi form ko 'processing' stamp laga deta hai submit karte hi (attempts++), phir kaam ke liye bahar jaata hai (await) -- agar woh kaam karte waqt gir bhi jaaye (exception), uska 'processing' stamp hata diya jaata hai wapas aane par (finally), taaki form stuck na reh jaaye.
how_it_works: try { attempts++; try { await provider.send() } catch { convert to failed result }; update status/lastError/nextAttemptAt } finally { dispatching.delete(key) }.
in_this_project: src/scheduler.ts::dispatchChannel exact code. test/tick.test.ts ka 'a provider that throws is treated as a failed attempt, not a crash, and does not affect other channels' isi try/catch ko prove karta hai.
advantages: Single await, easy to reason about exactly what can interleave
finally guarantees the dispatching guard never leaks even on an unexpected throw
disadvantages: attempts++ before await means a channel that later fails validation inside the try (it can't here, but conceptually) would still count as an attempt
common_mistakes: Incrementing attempts AFTER the await instead of before, which would break editPost's in-flight detection
Forgetting the inner try/catch, letting a provider throw crash the outer Promise.all for every channel in that tick()

question: How does the `dispatching` set work, and how do both tick() and cancelChannel/cancelPost use it?
answer_hinglish:
`dispatching` ek `Set<string>` hai, keys `"postId:channel"` format mein -- har entry batata hai ki is exact channel ka ek provider.send() abhi AWAIT ho raha hai, settle nahi hua hai.

tick() side: due channels nikalne ke baad, dispatch karne se PEHLE sab ke keys `dispatching.add()` ho jaate hain (loop mein), phir `Promise.all` se saare dispatchChannel() calls start hote hain. Due-detection filter mein bhi already `!this.dispatching.has(key)` check hota hai -- taaki ek channel jo already dispatch ho raha hai, usse dusri baar due na maana jaaye, ek dusre overlapping tick() call se.

cancelChannel/cancelPost side: `requireNotDispatching(postId, channel)` pehle call hota hai -- agar key dispatching set mein hai, DISPATCH_IN_PROGRESS throw hota hai, status change nahi hota. Yeh zaroori hai kyunki status 'pending' hi rehta hai poore send ke duration mein (attempts already increment ho chuka hota hai, par status abhi change nahi hua hota jab tak result na aa jaaye) -- isliye status check se yeh race detect nahi ho sakta, ek explicit guard chahiye.

Cleanup: dispatchChannel() ke finally block mein `dispatching.delete(key)` hamesha chalta hai, taaki guard permanently stuck na reh jaaye.
why_needed: attempts-already-incremented signal sirf editPost ke liye kaafi hai (because editPost checks attempts, not status); cancel ke liye status hi relevant hai jo send ke duration mein nahi badalta -- isliye cancel ko apna khud ka explicit marker chahiye.
real_world_analogy: Ek fitting room ka 'occupied' sign -- jab tak koi andar try kar raha hai, doosra customer use allot nahi kiya ja sakta, chahe outside se dikh rahe signs (jaise shoes bahar) kuch na bhi badlein. Khaali hone par sign hat jaata hai.
how_it_works: tick(): `due.forEach(... dispatching.add(key))` then `Promise.all(due.map(dispatchChannel))`. cancelChannel/cancelPost: `requireNotDispatching()` throws before any state mutation. dispatchChannel finally: `dispatching.delete(key)`.
in_this_project: src/scheduler.ts private field `dispatching = new Set<string>()`, methods tick(), requireNotDispatching(), dispatchChannel(). test/dispatch-guard.test.ts 'two overlapping tick() calls never dispatch the same due channel twice' aur 'cancelChannel refuses with DISPATCH_IN_PROGRESS while tick() is mid-send for that exact channel'.
advantages: One lightweight structure protects both the overlapping-tick() race and the cancel-during-send race
Guaranteed cleanup via finally, no leaked guard entries
disadvantages: Only protects against the SAME caller's overlap -- not designed for multiple separate worker processes sharing one scheduler instance
common_mistakes: Adding to dispatching after starting the send instead of before (would let two calls race into the same provider.send())
Forgetting to remove from dispatching on the failure path (only doing it on success) -- a stuck guard would permanently block that channel
follow_up_questions: Why must the dispatching.add() happen before the await, not after?
What test specifically proves this guard with a provider that never auto-resolves?
